Elamites
EE-lam-ites
n. pl. (the people of Elam, east of Babylonia; named twice)
Gentilic plural from Elam, a son of Shem (Genesis 10:22) and the region east of Babylonia that bore his name; Ezra 4:9 and Acts 2:9.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

The Elamites are named twice, and the two occurrences stand at opposite ends of the story. The first has them among the peoples who wrote to the Persian court against the rebuilding of Jerusalem: “Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites” (Ezra 4:9). The second has them in Jerusalem at Pentecost, hearing the gospel: “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia” (Acts 2:9), and what they heard is stated plainly: “Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Acts 2:11). The nation descends from Shem: “The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram” (Genesis 10:22). A people who had signed a letter to stop the building of the temple were, five centuries later, among the first to hear in their own tongue that the true temple had been raised in three days.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Elamites, the people of Elam, a region east of Babylonia; named at Ezra 4:9 and Acts 2:9.

expand to see more

Elamites is a gentilic plural from Elam.

Elam was a son of Shem, Genesis 10:22.

The region lay east of Babylonia, with Shushan as a chief city.

It occurs twice, at Ezra 4:9 and Acts 2:9.

Elamites were among those present in Jerusalem at Pentecost.

Key Scripture

Ezr 4:9 — "Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites,"

Act 2:9 — "Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia,"

Act 2:11 — "Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God."

Gen 10:22 — "The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram."

Modern Corruption

Pentecost is reduced to an ecstatic episode or to a symbol of diversity, where Acts 2 describes understood languages and a preached message.

expand to see more

Two readings of Pentecost are common and both miss the text. The first makes the tongues unintelligible ecstatic utterance; but the hearers say they heard “in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Acts 2:11), and the list of nations exists to prove the languages were real. The second makes the day a celebration of diversity as such; but the chapter is a sermon from Joel and the Psalms ending in a call to repent and be baptized, and three thousand were added. The miracle served the preaching; it did not replace it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reversal of Babel. At Babel one language was divided and men were scattered; at Pentecost many languages were given one message and men were gathered. The Elamites who once wrote to stop a building heard, in their own speech, of the One who is the foundation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Gentilic from Elam, son of Shem; Ezra 4:9, Acts 2:9.

Gentilic plural formed from Elam.

Elam is named among the sons of Shem at Genesis 10:22.

The region lay east of Babylonia.

Named at Ezra 4:9 among the opponents of the rebuilding.

Named at Acts 2:9 among the nations present at Pentecost.
